claim: Traditional drug safety assessment often fails to predict complications in humans, especially when the drug targets the immune system.
source: Traditional drug safety assessment often fails to predict complications in humans, especially when the drug targets the immune system.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract about limitations of traditional safety assessment methods.

claim: TCBs are associated with an on-target, off-tumor risk due to low levels of expression of tumor antigens in healthy tissues.
source: Although promising for cancer immunotherapy, TCBs are associated with an on-target, off-tumor risk due to low levels of expression of tumor antigens in healthy tissues.
evidence: This statement describes a known characteristic of TCBs based on established understanding of their mechanism.

claim: The Lung-Chip and Intestine-Chip could reproduce and predict target-dependent TCB safety liabilities.
source: We discovered that the Lung-Chip and Intestine-Chip could reproduce and predict target-dependent TCB safety liabilities, based on sensitivity to key determinants thereof, such as target expression and antibody affinity.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The Lung-Chip and Intestine-Chip are sensitive to key determinants of TCB safety liabilities such as target expression and antibody affinity.
source: We discovered that the Lung-Chip and Intestine-Chip could reproduce and predict target-dependent TCB safety liabilities, based on sensitivity to key determinants thereof, such as target expression and antibody affinity.
evidence: This finding is supported by dose-response experiments and comparisons between high and low affinity TCBs shown in Figures 2-4.

claim: Cancer immunotherapy has received intense attention over the past two decades owing to the promise of delivering durable cures by harnessing the cytotoxic potential of the immune system against tumor cells.
source: Cancer immunotherapy has received intense attention over the past two decades owing to the promise of delivering durable cures by harnessing the cytotoxic potential of the immune system against tumor cells (Waldman et al., 2020; Yang, 2015; Gong et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Only a fraction of patients responds to cancer immunotherapy.
source: However, although impressive improvement in long-term survival has been reported (Hodi et al., 2010; Schadendorf et al., 2015; Wolchok et al., 2017), only a fraction of patients responds.
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Systemic immunomodulation mediated by cancer immunotherapy drugs often elicits immune-related adverse events (irAEs), including skin and liver toxicity, colitis, and pneumonitis.
source: Furthermore, the systemic immunomodulation mediated by these drugs often elicits immune-related adverse events (irAEs), including skin and liver toxicity, colitis, and pneumonitis, limiting their broad clinical application in battling cancer (Champiat et al., 2017; Naidoo et al., 2015; Kennedy and Salama, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature on adverse events.

claim: T-cell engaging bispecific antibodies (TCBs) are a novel class of cancer immunotherapeutic agents that have the potential to improve on the clinical efficacy and safety of traditional immunotherapy.
source: T-cell engaging bispecific antibodies (TCBs) are a novel class of cancer immunotherapeutic agents that have the potential to improve on the clinical efficacy and safety of traditional immunotherapy (Clynes and Desjarlais, 2019; Labrijn et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to literature on TCBs.

claim: TCBs exert their anti-tumor activity by simultaneously binding to a cancer surface antigen and the CD3 T-cell receptor, thereby both activating the latter and physically crosslinking it to target cells.
source: TCBs exert their anti-tumor activity by simultaneously binding to a cancer surface antigen and the CD3 T-cell receptor, thereby both activating the latter and physically crosslinking it to target cells (Bacac et al., 2016a).
evidence: This describes the mechanism of action of TCBs, supported by a citation.

claim: TCBs can recruit and activate T cells independently of their T-cell receptor specificity.
source: This synthetic immunity approach is particularly favorable for targeting less immunogenic, neo-antigen-lacking tumors, as T cells can be recruited and activated independently of their T-cell receptor specificity.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the TCB mechanism of action described in the manuscript.

claim: Strictly tumor-targeted immunomodulation by TCBs is expected to reduce the systemic inflammatory toxicities associated with traditional immunotherapies.
source: This strictly tumor-targeted immunomodulation is also expected to reduce the systemic inflammatory toxicities associated with traditional immunotherapies.
evidence: This is a theoretical expectation based on the mechanism of TCBs.

claim: A large number of TCB molecules targeting solid and blood tumors are currently in various stages of clinical evaluation.
source: The therapeutic potential of TCBs is exemplified by the large number of molecules targeting solid and blood tumors, which are currently in various stages of clinical evaluation (Ishiguro et al., 2017; Goebeler and Bargou, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to literature on clinical development of TCBs.

claim: The antigens targeted by TCBs are rarely exclusive to the tumor, but are also often expressed, albeit at lower levels, in normal tissues.
source: The antigens targeted are rarely exclusive to the tumor, but are also often expressed, albeit at lower levels, in normal tissues, rendering TCBs subject to 'on-target, off-tumor' safety liabilities.
evidence: This is a general statement about TCB target expression patterns, supported by knowledge in the field.

claim: A Bispecific T-cell Engager (BiTE) targeted to EGFR produced severe liver and kidney toxicities in non-human primates, in line with EGFR expression in these organs, and led to the termination of the animals.
source: For example, a Bispecific T-cell Engager (BiTE) targeted to the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) produced severe liver and kidney toxicities in non-human primates, in line with EGFR expression in these organs, and led to the termination of the animals (Klinger et al., 2016; Lutterbuese et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an example of TCB toxicity from published literature.

claim: An EpCAM-targeted BiTE triggered severe diarrhea in a Phase I clinical study, consistent with the expression of EpCAM in the gastrointestinal tract.
source: Clinical adverse events were reported in a recent Phase I study evaluating an epithelial cell adhesion molecule (EpCAM)-targeted BiTE as a therapy for a variety of epithelial carcinomas. Consistent with the expression of EpCAM in the gastrointestinal tract, the molecule triggered severe diarrhea and ultimately prevented escalation to efficacious doses and the identification of a therapeutic window (Kebenko et al., 2018; Trabolsi et al., 2019).
evidence: This clinical example is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Traditional rodent-based preclinical models are often ill-suited for predicting some cancer immunotherapy-mediated adverse events in humans in part because of the fundamental differences in the immunological responses between the species.
source: Traditional rodent-based preclinical models are often ill-suited for predicting some cancer immunotherapy-mediated adverse events in humans in part because of the fundamental differences in the immunological responses between the species (Bjornson-Hooper et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to literature on species differences.

claim: The severity of diarrhea elicited by an EpCAM-targeted BiTE was not predicted by preclinical studies in mice.
source: In the EpCAM example mentioned above, the severity of the diarrhea elicited by the treatment was not predicted by preclinical studies in mice (Brischwein et al., 2006).
evidence: This is an example of failure of mouse models, supported by a citation.

claim: An increasing number of TCBs target human-specific antigens that lack expression in animals, rendering preclinical animal studies uninformative for safety and efficacy assessments.
source: Moreover, an increasing number of TCBs target human-specific antigens that lack expression in animals, rendering preclinical animal studies uninformative for safety and efficacy assessments (Bacac et al., 2016a).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and describes a limitation of animal models.

claim: The development of preclinical models that better translate to human immunity is regarded as one of the top current challenges of cancer immunotherapy.
source: Indeed, the development of preclinical models that better translate to human immunity is regarded as one of the top current challenges of cancer immunotherapy (Hegde and Chen, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to literature on challenges in the field.

claim: Conventional in vitro two-dimensional (2D) models fail to provide the complexity required to model the biological mechanisms of immunotherapeutic effects.
source: While human-relevant cell-based models of tissues and organs promise to bridge this gap, conventional in vitro two-dimensional (2D) models fail to provide the complexity required to model the biological mechanisms of immunotherapeutic effects.
evidence: This is a general statement about limitations of 2D models based on established knowledge.

claim: The reductive microenvironment of 2D models, devoid of essential cellular, biochemical, and biophysical factors found in the native organ, precludes the expression of TCB targets at physiologically relevant levels and patterns.
source: Furthermore, their reductive microenvironment, devoid of essential cellular, biochemical, and biophysical factors found in the native organ, precludes the expression of TCB targets at physiologically relevant levels and patterns, crucial for capturing TCB pharmacology and safety liabilities.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the limitations of 2D models based on their characteristics.

claim: Organ-on-Chip models combine micro-engineering with cultured primary human cells to recreate the complex multifactorial microenvironment and functions of native tissues and organs.
source: Organ-on-Chip models aim to overcome these limitations by combining micro-engineering with cultured primary human cells to recreate the complex multifactorial microenvironment and functions of native tissues and organs (Huh et al., 2010).
evidence: This describes the general approach of Organ-on-Chip technology, supported by a citation.

claim: Organs-on-Chips that model key functional aspects of tissue-level physiology have been shown to more accurately capture in vivo-relevant phenotypes.
source: Organs-on-Chips model key functional aspects of tissue-level physiology such as epithelial and microvascular tissue-tissue interfaces, and physiologically relevant mechanical forces, have been shown to more accurately capture in vivo-relevant phenotypes (Kasendra et al., 2020; Kasendra et al., 2018; Gayer and Basson, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published studies on Organ-on-Chip technology.

claim: FOLR1 is overexpressed in many solid, epithelial-derived tumors including ovarian, lung, and breast cancer.
source: FOLR1 is overexpressed in many solid, epithelial-derived tumors including ovarian, lung, and breast cancer (Scaranti et al., 2020), but is also expressed to a lower degree on normal epithelial cells as found in the lung and kidneys (Parker et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement about FOLR1 expression is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: FOLR1 is expressed to a lower degree on normal epithelial cells as found in the lung and kidneys.
source: FOLR1 is overexpressed in many solid, epithelial-derived tumors including ovarian, lung, and breast cancer (Scaranti et al., 2020), but is also expressed to a lower degree on normal epithelial cells as found in the lung and kidneys (Parker et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement about FOLR1 expression in normal tissues is supported by a citation.

claim: A high-affinity FOLR1-TCB (FOLR1(Hi) TCB) was efficacious in human breast cancer patient-derived xenograft models.
source: While a high-affinity FOLR1-TCB (FOLR1(Hi) TCB) was efficacious in human breast cancer patient-derived xenograft models (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), severe on-target toxicity in the lung of cynomolgus monkey was observed (AMea, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: FOLR1(Hi) TCB caused severe on-target toxicity in the lung of cynomolgus monkey.
source: While a high-affinity FOLR1-TCB (FOLR1(Hi) TCB) was efficacious in human breast cancer patient-derived xenograft models (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), severe on-target toxicity in the lung of cynomolgus monkey was observed (AMea, 2016).
evidence: This toxicity observation is supported by a citation and histopathology data in Figure 1A.

claim: Clinical signs of severe respiratory inflammation appeared as early as 24 hr post-dosing with FOLR1(Hi) TCB in cynomolgus monkeys.
source: Clinical signs of severe respiratory inflammation appeared as early as 24 hr post-dosing, and pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-6, IL-2, and IL-8 were elevated in the blood of affected animals, and importantly coincided with an increase of inflammation markers.
evidence: This describes observations from the cynomolgus study.

claim: Pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-6, IL-2, and IL-8 were elevated in the blood of cynomolgus monkeys treated with FOLR1(Hi) TCB.
source: Clinical signs of severe respiratory inflammation appeared as early as 24 hr post-dosing, and pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-6, IL-2, and IL-8 were elevated in the blood of affected animals, and importantly coincided with an increase of inflammation markers.
evidence: This describes cytokine measurements from the cynomolgus study.

claim: Histopathology assessment revealed leukocytic infiltrates in lung tissue of cynomolgus monkeys treated with FOLR1(Hi) TCB, indicative of immune-mediated toxicity.
source: Histopathology assessment revealed leukocytic infiltrates in lung tissue indicative of immune-mediated toxicity (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by histopathology data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: IHC studies indicated low relative expression of FOLR1 target antigen in lung alveolar epithelial cells of cynomolgus lung tissue.
source: Further immunohistochemistry (IHC) studies (Figure 1B–D) indicated low relative expression (compared to high FOLR1 expression in the ovarian carcinoma cell line, HeLa) of the FOLR1 target antigen in lung alveolar epithelial cells of cynomolgus lung tissue suggesting an adverse event largely driven by on-target toxicity.
evidence: This is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 1B-D.

claim: IHC analysis of FOLR1 expression in the human lung revealed similar levels and patterns of the antigen as in the cynomolgus.
source: Importantly, IHC analysis of FOLR1 expression in the human lung revealed similar levels and patterns of the antigen as in the cynomolgus (Figure 1E,F), extending the threat of safety liabilities to patients in the clinical setting.
evidence: This is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 1E,F comparing human and cynomolgus lung tissue.

claim: FOLR1 gene expression was stable over time in the Alveolus Lung-Chip as shown by quantification of RNA transcripts.
source: FOLR1 gene expression was even over time as shown by quantification of RNA transcripts (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: FOLR1 protein expression was confirmed in mature Alveolus Lung-Chips.
source: We also confirmed FOLR1 protein expression in mature chips (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: The cell surface expression of FOLR1 within the Alveolus Lung-Chip was estimated at an average of ~10,000 molecules expressed per cell.
source: Flow cytometry-mediated quantification allowed us to estimate the cell surface expression of FOLR1 within the Alveolus Lung-Chip at an average of ~10,000 molecules expressed per cell (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: The high FOLR1 expressing ovarian carcinoma HeLa cell line displayed an average of ~450,000 molecules per cell when cultured on chip.
source: For comparison, the high FOLR1 expressing ovarian carcinoma HeLa cell line displayed an average of ~450,000 molecules per cell when cultured on chip (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), confirming the difference observed in IHC between healthy and tumor cells.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: FOLR1(Hi) TCB treated chips presented an increased apoptosis of the alveolar epithelium compared to chips treated with a non-targeting (NT) TCB control antibody.
source: Compared to the chips treated with a non-targeting (NT) TCB control antibody, FOLR1(Hi) TCB treated chips presented an increased apoptosis of the alveolar epithelium (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: FOLR1(Hi) TCB treatment led to increased T-cell activation (as evidenced by CD69 upregulation in CD8+ T cells) in the presence of target-expressing cells.
source: Consistently, FOLR1(Hi) TCB treatment led to increased T-cell activation (as evidenced by CD69 upregulation in CD8+ T cells) in the presence of target-expressing cells (Figure 2C), but not in PBMC only (Figure 2C, right panel).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: FOLR1(Hi) TCB did not induce T-cell activation in PBMC only (without target-expressing cells).
source: Consistently, FOLR1(Hi) TCB treatment led to increased T-cell activation (as evidenced by CD69 upregulation in CD8+ T cells) in the presence of target-expressing cells (Figure 2C), but not in PBMC only (Figure 2C, right panel).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2C, right panel.

claim: FOLR1(Hi) TCB treatment resulted in significantly increased secretion of IFNγ at 24 hr and 48 hr.
source: Supernatants collected from the outlet reservoir of the epithelial channels at 24 and 48 hr post-treatment were measured for multiplex cytokines (Figure 2D), revealing a significantly increased secretion of IFNγ at 24 hr and 48 hr that correlated with increased granzyme B and IL-6 at 48 hr in response to FOLR1(Hi) TCB.
evidence: This is supported by multiplex cytokine data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: FOLR1(Hi) TCB treatment resulted in increased granzyme B and IL-6 at 48 hr.
source: Supernatants collected from the outlet reservoir of the epithelial channels at 24 and 48 hr post-treatment were measured for multiplex cytokines (Figure 2D), revealing a significantly increased secretion of IFNγ at 24 hr and 48 hr that correlated with increased granzyme B and IL-6 at 48 hr in response to FOLR1(Hi) TCB.
evidence: This is supported by multiplex cytokine data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: FOLR1(Hi) TCB treatment led to increased attachment of both T cells and non CD3+ cells to the target epithelium.
source: Quantification of the immune cell presence in fixed chips confirmed increased attachment of both T cells and non CD3+ cells to the target epithelium in the FOLR1(Hi) TCB condition (Figure 2E,F), which is consistent with the TCB mode of action, whereby immune cells are crosslinked to target cells.
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2E,F.

claim: The Alveolus Lung-Chip successfully replicates aspects of the FOLR1(Hi) TCB-mediated toxicity observed in cynomolgus.
source: Together, these data suggest that the Alveolus Lung-Chip successfully replicates aspects of the FOLR1 (Hi) TCB-mediated toxicity observed in cynomolgus, and suggests that the human lung would be subject to similar safety liabilities.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data comparing chip results to cynomolgus toxicity.

claim: The human lung would be subject to similar safety liabilities as observed in cynomolgus with FOLR1(Hi) TCB.
source: Together, these data suggest that the Alveolus Lung-Chip successfully replicates aspects of the FOLR1 (Hi) TCB-mediated toxicity observed in cynomolgus, and suggests that the human lung would be subject to similar safety liabilities.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity of FOLR1 expression patterns and chip responses.

claim: All concentrations of FOLR1(Hi) TCB starting from 2 ng/mL induced significant T-cell activation in HeLa chips.
source: Although no effects were seen at the lowest concentration, all concentrations starting from 2 ng/mL induced significant T-cell activation (measured at 48 hr), cancer cell apoptosis (from 24 hr onwards) and strong cytokine release, as expected from the high level of FOLR1 expression in HeLa cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: FOLR1(Hi) TCB EC50 in HeLa chips was estimated at 1.1 pM, which was close to the value obtained from standard 2D in vitro killing experiments (2.2 pM).
source: Of note, FOLR1(Hi) TCB EC50 was estimated at 1.1 pM, which was close to the value obtained from standard 2D in vitro killing experiments (2.2 pM).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of EC50 values between chip and 2D assays.

claim: FOLR1(Lo) TCB presented a lower binding to FOLR1-expressing HeLa cells while retaining a potent killing activity in coculture assays and an in vivo tumor control efficacy.
source: As a result of that design, FOLR1(Lo) TCB presented a lower binding to FOLR1-expressing HeLa cells while retaining a potent killing activity in coculture assays and an in vivo tumor control efficacy (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E-G.

claim: FOLR1(Hi) TCB induced a significant increase in all readouts starting at the 0.2 μg/mL concentration in the Alveolus Lung-Chip.
source: We profiled the two TCBs, FOLR1(Hi) and FOLR1 (Lo), in the immunocompetent Alveolus Lung-Chip following the workflow and readouts described above, and found that FOLR1(Hi) TCB induced a significant increase in all the readouts starting at the 0.2 μg/mL concentration whereas FOLR1(Lo) TCB showed a response only at the highest concentration of 20 μg/mL and to a much lower magnitude than the high-affinity molecule (Figure 3A–D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 3A-D.

claim: FOLR1(Lo) TCB showed a response only at the highest concentration of 20 μg/mL and to a much lower magnitude than the high-affinity molecule in the Alveolus Lung-Chip.
source: We profiled the two TCBs, FOLR1(Hi) and FOLR1 (Lo), in the immunocompetent Alveolus Lung-Chip following the workflow and readouts described above, and found that FOLR1(Hi) TCB induced a significant increase in all the readouts starting at the 0.2 μg/mL concentration whereas FOLR1(Lo) TCB showed a response only at the highest concentration of 20 μg/mL and to a much lower magnitude than the high-affinity molecule (Figure 3A–D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 3A-D.

claim: The cellular responses on the Alveolus Lung-Chip platform are sensitive to differences in antibody affinity.
source: These results demonstrated that the cellular responses on the platform are sensitive to differences in antibody affinity and recapitulates the biology associated with the mode of action of TCBs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of FOLR1(Hi) and FOLR1(Lo) TCB responses.

claim: The lower affinity FOLR1 TCB did not cause lung inflammation in cynomolgus monkeys.
source: Following these in vitro observations, the lower affinity FOLR1 TCB was tested in a cynomolgus toxicology study and none of the animals experienced the lung inflammation observed with FOLR1(Hi) TCB (Figure 3E), confirming the safer profile predicted by the Alveolus Lung-Chip.
evidence: This is supported by histopathology data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The Alveolus Lung-Chip correctly predicted the safer profile of FOLR1(Lo) TCB confirmed in cynomolgus studies.
source: Following these in vitro observations, the lower affinity FOLR1 TCB was tested in a cynomolgus toxicology study and none of the animals experienced the lung inflammation observed with FOLR1(Hi) TCB (Figure 3E), confirming the safer profile predicted by the Alveolus Lung-Chip.
evidence: This is a validation of the chip's predictive capability based on concordance with in vivo data.

claim: In the transwell environment, quantification of TCB-dependent immune cell attachment and apoptosis did not show differences between the control and FOLR1 TCB treatment conditions.
source: In the transwell environment, quantification of TCB-dependent immune cell attachment and apoptosis did not show differences between the control and FOLR1 TCB treatment conditions.
evidence: This is supported by comparison data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The transwell version did not capture differences between FOLR1 antibodies: FOLR1(Lo) TCB led to a higher amount of granzyme B and IFNγ release than the chips, which is inconsistent with the absence of toxicity observed in vivo.
source: Also, the transwell version did not capture differences between FOLR1 antibodies: FOLR1(Lo) TCB led to a higher amount of granzyme B and IFNγ release than the chips, which is inconsistent with the absence of toxicity observed in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by comparison data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The Alveolar Lung-Chip platform can faithfully evaluate TCB on-target, off-tumor risks and presents a superior value to existing alternatives.
source: Given the higher concordance of the results produced by the Alveolar Lung-Chip compared with the transwell counterpart, we propose that the novel immunocompetent Alveolus Lung-Chip platform can faithfully evaluate TCB on-target, off-tumor risks and presents a superior value to the existing alternatives.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of chip and transwell performance.

claim: CEA is overexpressed in a range of solid tumors, including colorectal cancer.
source: In this example, we focused on TCBs targeting carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), which is overexpressed in a range of solid tumors, including colorectal cancer (Hammarström, 1999).
evidence: This statement about CEA expression is supported by a citation.

claim: CEA(Hi) and CEA(Lo) TCB are potent mediators of tumor cell lysis and T-cell activation in vitro.
source: Indeed, we have found that CEA(Hi) and CEA(Lo) TCB are potent mediators of tumor cell lysis and T-cell activation in vitro (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C), and exhibit robust anti-tumor activity in humanized mice engrafted with CEA-expressing tumors (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: CEA(Hi) and CEA(Lo) TCB exhibit robust anti-tumor activity in humanized mice engrafted with CEA-expressing tumors.
source: Indeed, we have found that CEA(Hi) and CEA(Lo) TCB are potent mediators of tumor cell lysis and T-cell activation in vitro (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C), and exhibit robust anti-tumor activity in humanized mice engrafted with CEA-expressing tumors (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: CEA is expressed in the gastrointestinal tract.
source: Aside from solid tumors, however, CEA is expressed in the gastrointestinal tract (Benchimol et al., 1989; Thomas et al., 1995; Zhou et al., 1993).
evidence: This statement about CEA expression is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Immunohistochemistry analysis of primary human intestinal samples confirmed high expression of CEA in the colon, whereas small intestinal expression was lower.
source: Immunohistochemistry analysis of primary human intestinal samples confirmed high expression of CEA in the colon, whereas small intestinal expression was lower.
evidence: This is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In both colon and small intestine tissues, CEA was enriched on the apical surface of the barrier.
source: In both tissues, CEA was enriched on the apical surface of the barrier (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: CEA-targeting TCBs showed lack of cross-reactivity to cynomolgus monkey CEA.
source: Our antibodies recognize a human-specific epitope within the CEA protein,, making mice and cynomolgus preclinical toxicology models unsuitable for the assessment of toxicities caused by CEA-targeting TCBs. Indeed, our antibodies showed lack of cross-reactivity to cynomolgus monkey CEA, which underscores the need for human-relevant models in addressing this question (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by binding data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Immunofluorescence analysis revealed robust expression of CEA in the Colon Intestine-Chip epithelium.
source: Immunofluorescence analysis revealed robust expression of CEA in the Colon Intestine-Chip epithelium, whereas expression in the Duodenum Intestine-Chip appeared weaker and localized to the apical surface (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: CEA expression in the Duodenum Intestine-Chip appeared weaker and localized to the apical surface.
source: Immunofluorescence analysis revealed robust expression of CEA in the Colon Intestine-Chip epithelium, whereas expression in the Duodenum Intestine-Chip appeared weaker and localized to the apical surface (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Flow cytometry-mediated quantification verified higher target abundance in the Colon-Chip compared with the Duodenum-chip.
source: Flow cytometry-mediated quantification verified the cell surface expression of CEA within the Intestine-Chip and confirmed the higher target abundance in the Colon-Chip compared with the Duodenum-chip (Figure 4C), in line with the regional differences observed in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The regional differences in CEA expression in the Intestine-Chips are in line with the regional differences observed in vivo.
source: Flow cytometry-mediated quantification verified the cell surface expression of CEA within the Intestine-Chip and confirmed the higher target abundance in the Colon-Chip compared with the Duodenum-chip (Figure 4C), in line with the regional differences observed in vivo.
evidence: This is a comparison between chip data and in vivo observations.

claim: Colon and duodenum organoids cultured in the conventional 3D format featured target expression levels similar to those measured in the chips.
source: To our surprise, colon and duodenum organoids cultured in the conventional 3D format featured target expression levels similar to those measured in the chips (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The Intestine-Chip is more suitable for the assessment of on-target TCB toxicities than conventional 3D organoids, given the more physiologically accurate CEA expression patterns.
source: Nonetheless, despite the similarity in target abundance, we believe that the Intestine-Chip is more suitable for the assessment of on-target TCB toxicities, given the more physiologically accurate CEA expression patterns compared with those observed in organoids.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of expression patterns between chips and organoids.

claim: Immunofluorescence analysis revealed apical enrichment of CEA in the Colon-Chip (strong) and Duodenum-chip (weak).
source: Immunofluorescence analysis revealed the familiar apical enrichment of CEA in the Colon-Chip (strong) and Duodenum-chip (weak) (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B), whereas CEA appeared to be junctional and non-polarized in colon organoids.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3B.

claim: CEA appeared to be junctional and non-polarized in colon organoids.
source: Immunofluorescence analysis revealed the familiar apical enrichment of CEA in the Colon-Chip (strong) and Duodenum-chip (weak) (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B), whereas CEA appeared to be junctional and non-polarized in colon organoids.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The incorporation of microenvironmental cues, including flow and peristalsis, has shown to lead to enhanced maturation within the Intestine-Chip.
source: Indeed, the incorporation of microenvironmental cues, including flow and peristalsis, has shown to lead to enhanced maturation within the Intestine-Chip (Kasendra et al., 2020; Kasendra et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published studies on Intestine-Chip maturation.

claim: A commercial 2D model comprising primary intestinal epithelial cells showed patchy CEA expression, which appeared weaker than that observed in the native colon.
source: Importantly, immunohistochemistry analysis of a commercial 2D model comprising primary intestinal epithelial cells showed patchy CEA expression, which appeared weaker than that observed in the native colon (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3C.

claim: The commercial 2D intestinal model had an average of about 2000 CEA surface binding sites per cell.
source: Consistently, we estimated an average of about 2000 CEA surface binding sites per cell in this system (Figure 4—figure supplement 3D), which is dramatically lower than the expression recorded in the Colon Intestine-Chip.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3D.

claim: Both CEA(Hi) and CEA(Lo) TCB induced dose-dependent increase in PBMC attachment in the Colon Intestine-Chip.
source: Both CEA(Hi) and CEA(Lo) TCB induced dose-dependent increase in PBMC attachment (Figure 4D) and activation, as evidenced by CD69 upregulation (Figure 4E) and the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including granzyme B, IFNγ, and IL-6 (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Both CEA(Hi) and CEA(Lo) TCB induced dose-dependent increase in PBMC activation, as evidenced by CD69 upregulation.
source: Both CEA(Hi) and CEA(Lo) TCB induced dose-dependent increase in PBMC attachment (Figure 4D) and activation, as evidenced by CD69 upregulation (Figure 4E) and the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including granzyme B, IFNγ, and IL-6 (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Both CEA(Hi) and CEA(Lo) TCB induced the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including granzyme B, IFNγ, and IL-6.
source: Both CEA(Hi) and CEA(Lo) TCB induced dose-dependent increase in PBMC attachment (Figure 4D) and activation, as evidenced by CD69 upregulation (Figure 4E) and the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including granzyme B, IFNγ, and IL-6 (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by multiplex cytokine data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: CEA(Hi) TCB triggered higher PBMC attachment, activation and cytokine release compared with CEA(Lo) TCB.
source: As expected, CEA(Hi) TCB triggered higher PBMC attachment, activation and cytokine release compared with CEA(Lo) TCB, confirming that the model is sensitive to differences in antibody affinity, which would be expected to translate into differential toxicity outcomes in the clinic.
evidence: This is a comparison of responses between high and low affinity TCBs in the Colon Intestine-Chip.

claim: The Colon Intestine-Chip model is sensitive to differences in antibody affinity.
source: As expected, CEA(Hi) TCB triggered higher PBMC attachment, activation and cytokine release compared with CEA(Lo) TCB, confirming that the model is sensitive to differences in antibody affinity, which would be expected to translate into differential toxicity outcomes in the clinic.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of CEA(Hi) and CEA(Lo) TCB responses.

claim: No activation was observed upon treatment with an antibody that engages the CD3 receptor on T cells but cannot bind to CEA (NT TCB).
source: Importantly, we observed no activation upon treatment with an antibody that engages the CD3 receptor on T cells but cannot bind to CEA (NT TCB).
evidence: This is supported by data showing no response to NT TCB in the Intestine-Chip.

claim: The CEA-targeting TCBs failed to induce activation of PBMC only, in the absence of target tissue.
source: Likewise, the CEA-targeting TCBs failed to induce activation of PBMC only, in the absence of target tissue (Figure 4—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3E.

claim: The effects observed in the Intestine-Chips are target dependent and mode of action dependent.
source: Together, these data confirm that the effects observed in the chips are target dependent and mode of action dependent, ruling out non-specific PBMC activation and cytokine release mediated by CD3 engagement only.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from control experiments with NT TCB and PBMC only.

claim: CD69 expression and cytokine release induced by both TCBs were significantly attenuated in the Duodenum Intestine-Chip compared to the Colon Intestine-Chip, in line with the lower target expression.
source: Indeed, we observed differences in on-target toxicity governed by target abundance: CD69 expression and cytokine release induced by both TCBs were significantly attenuated in the Duodenum Intestine-Chip, in line with the lower target expression (Figure 4G–H).
evidence: This is supported by comparison data shown in Figure 4G-H.

claim: CEA(Lo) TCB induced minimal increase in CD69 expression and no cytokine release in the Duodenum Intestine-Chip, relative to the non-targeting TCB.
source: The reduction was more extensive in the case of CEA(Lo) TCB, which induced minimal increase in CD69 expression and no cytokine release, relative to the non-targeting TCB.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4G-H comparing Duodenum responses.

claim: CEA(Hi) TCB induced PBMC activation and cytokine release in the Duodenum Intestine-Chip which were significantly elevated compared with the non-targeting control.
source: CEA(Hi) TCB induced PBMC activation and cytokine release which, while lower than those observed in the Colon Intestine-Chip, were significantly elevated compared with the non-targeting control, suggesting that the high-affinity molecule may pose safety risks even in tissues with low target expression as described for the high-affinity FOLR1 molecule in the lung.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4G-H.

claim: The high-affinity CEA molecule may pose safety risks even in tissues with low target expression.
source: CEA(Hi) TCB induced PBMC activation and cytokine release which, while lower than those observed in the Colon Intestine-Chip, were significantly elevated compared with the non-targeting control, suggesting that the high-affinity molecule may pose safety risks even in tissues with low target expression as described for the high-affinity FOLR1 molecule in the lung.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Duodenum Intestine-Chip data and comparison to FOLR1 findings.

claim: The Alveolus Lung-Chip successfully recapitulated FOLR1 TCB-mediated lung toxicities observed in cynomolgus monkeys.
source: We demonstrate that the Alveolus Lung-Chip successfully recapitulated FOLR1 TCB-mediated lung toxicities observed in cynomolgus monkeys and instructed the design of a second-generation molecule, whose favorable lung safety profile predicted by the chip model was verified in vivo.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings for the Lung-Chip.

claim: The Alveolus Lung-Chip instructed the design of a second-generation FOLR1 molecule, whose favorable lung safety profile predicted by the chip model was verified in vivo.
source: We demonstrate that the Alveolus Lung-Chip successfully recapitulated FOLR1 TCB-mediated lung toxicities observed in cynomolgus monkeys and instructed the design of a second-generation molecule, whose favorable lung safety profile predicted by the chip model was verified in vivo.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the validation of the Lung-Chip's predictive capability.

claim: The Intestine-Chip model captured the liabilities of a TCB targeting a human-specific antigen.
source: The Intestine-Chip model captured the liabilities of a TCB targeting a human-specific antigen, thus filling the gap left by the lack of cross-reactivity in animals and suitable animal models overall.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings for the Intestine-Chip.

claim: The Intestine-Chip model displayed sensitivity to TCB affinity.
source: The model likewise displayed sensitivity to TCB affinity and predicted differential, target expression-dependent toxicity outcomes between different intestinal regions.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the Intestine-Chip's capabilities.

claim: The Intestine-Chip model predicted differential, target expression-dependent toxicity outcomes between different intestinal regions.
source: The model likewise displayed sensitivity to TCB affinity and predicted differential, target expression-dependent toxicity outcomes between different intestinal regions.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the Intestine-Chip's capabilities.

claim: Both the Lung-Chip and the Intestine-Chip were able to shed light into the toxicity mechanisms of the molecules, clearly decoupling target-mediated effects from T cell activation through CD3 engagement only.
source: Both models were able to shed light into the toxicity mechanisms of the molecules, clearly decoupling target-mediated effects from T cell activation through CD3 engagement only, which has been shown to be an additional mode of TCB-induced adverse events (Segal et al., 1999).
evidence: This is a summary statement of the mechanistic insights provided by the models.

claim: T cell activation through CD3 engagement only has been shown to be an additional mode of TCB-induced adverse events.
source: Both models were able to shed light into the toxicity mechanisms of the molecules, clearly decoupling target-mediated effects from T cell activation through CD3 engagement only, which has been shown to be an additional mode of TCB-induced adverse events (Segal et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The Alveolus Lung-Chip was found to report more specific TCB-responses and provide additional important readouts compared with transwell-based approaches.
source: It is worth mentioning that both the Lung-Chip and the Intestine-Chip demonstrated an advantage over conventional models for this application: the Alveolus Lung-Chip was found to report more specific TCB-responses and provide additional important readouts compared with transwell-based approaches, whereas the Intestine-Chip supported more physiologically relevant target expression, compared with both 3D organoids and primary intestinal barrier grown in transwells.
evidence: This is a summary statement comparing the Lung-Chip to transwell models.

claim: The Intestine-Chip supported more physiologically relevant target expression, compared with both 3D organoids and primary intestinal barrier grown in transwells.
source: It is worth mentioning that both the Lung-Chip and the Intestine-Chip demonstrated an advantage over conventional models for this application: the Alveolus Lung-Chip was found to report more specific TCB-responses and provide additional important readouts compared with transwell-based approaches, whereas the Intestine-Chip supported more physiologically relevant target expression, compared with both 3D organoids and primary intestinal barrier grown in transwells.
evidence: This is a summary statement comparing the Intestine-Chip to other models.

claim: 'On-target, off-tumor' TCB safety liabilities have in some cases been only detected either in late-stage preclinical models (non-human primates) or as life-threatening adverse events in the clinic.
source: Owing to the absence of predictive early-stage assays, 'on-target, off-tumor' TCB safety liabilities have in some cases been only detected either in late-stage preclinical models (non-human primates) or as life-threatening adverse events in the clinic.
evidence: This is a general statement about the current state of TCB safety assessment.

claim: Advanced human cellular models that capture the immunopathology of TCB-induced adverse events would aid the iterative antibody design at the early stage.
source: Advanced human cellular models that capture the immunopathology of TCB-induced adverse events would aid the iterative antibody design at the early stage, thus ensuring favorable safety profiles before entering clinical trials, reducing attrition rates, and ultimately expediting the application of these potentially life-saving therapies.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential value of the models described in the manuscript.

claim: The mechanistic insights into on-target, off-tumor toxicities and design opportunities afforded by these platforms are not restricted to T-cell engagers like TCBs, but also apply to chimeric antigen receptor T (CART) cell therapy.
source: Importantly, the mechanistic insights into on-target, off-tumor toxicities and design opportunities afforded by these platforms are not restricted to T-cell engagers like TCBs, but also apply to chimeric antigen receptor T (CART) cell therapy, bearing in mind their similar modes of action.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity of mechanisms between TCBs and CART cells.

claim: A human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (Her2) CART therapy led to lethal toxicity through off-tumor cardiopulmonary targeting in a patient with colorectal cancer.
source: For instance, a human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (Her2) CART therapy, intended to treat a patient with colorectal cancer, led to lethal toxicity through off-tumor cardiopulmonary targeting (Morgan et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an example from published literature, supported by a citation.

claim: A Her2 CART therapy was affinity-tuned to detect tumor cells with a high density of surface antigens, while sparing normal cells with lower antigen expression.
source: To improve its efficacy-safety profile, this therapy was affinity-tuned to detect tumor cells with a high density of surface antigens, while sparing normal cells with lower antigen expression (Zhao et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an example from published literature, supported by a citation.

claim: A mouse model expressing human Her2 was used to confirm the safer profile of the low-affinity CART.
source: A mouse model expressing human Her2 was used to confirm the safer profile of the low-affinity CART (Castellarin et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an example from published literature, supported by a citation.

claim: The Lung- and Intestine-Chips are fully human, applicable to various targets and faster to generate than humanized mouse models.
source: However, in contrast to the humanized mouse models, these in vitro tools are fully human, applicable to various targets and faster to generate, making them a promising alternative for antibody/CART preclinical safety testing, format selection, and optimization.
evidence: This is a comparison of the chip models to humanized mouse models.

claim: The immune-competent Organs-Chips can bridge preclinical research to clinical application, by aiding the discovery of early predictive biomarkers of TCB/CART toxicity in patients.
source: Furthermore, the immune-competent Organs-Chips described here can bridge preclinical research to clinical application, by aiding the discovery of early predictive biomarkers of TCB/CART toxicity in patients, which would certainly help to anticipate and manage life-threatening adverse events.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential future applications of the models.

claim: Early elevation of specific serum cytokines, including IFN-γ and IL-6, was found to precede the development of severe cytokine release syndrome in response to CART therapy.
source: For example, early elevation of specific serum cytokines, including IFN-γ and IL-6, was found to precede the development of severe cytokine release syndrome in response to CART therapy (Teachey et al., 2016; Hay, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature on CART toxicity biomarkers.

claim: The release of IFN-γ and IL-6 was consistently observed in both the Alveolus Lung and Colon Intestine-Chip upon treatment with high-affinity FOLR1 and CEA TCB, which led to on-target toxicity.
source: The release of IFN-γ and IL-6 was consistently observed in both the Alveolus Lung and Colon Intestine-Chip upon treatment with high-affinity FOLR1 and CEA TCB, which led to on-target toxicity.
evidence: This is a summary of cytokine data from the chip experiments.

claim: The detection of clinically relevant biomarkers in the chip models exemplifies the translational value of the platform.
source: The detection of such clinically relevant biomarkers exemplifies the translational value of our platform.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation of clinically relevant cytokines in the chips.

claim: The chip system could be coupled with unbiased proteomic analyses of chip supernatants and transcriptomic dissection of the effector and target cell pools to uncover early novel predictors of TCB-mediated adverse events.
source: Going forward, the system could be coupled with, for example, unbiased proteomic analyses of chip supernatants and transcriptomic dissection of the effector and target cell pools and used to uncover early novel predictors or TCB-mediated adverse events.
evidence: This is a statement about potential future applications of the platform.

claim: Testing the same TCB molecule in a healthy Lung-Chip versus a cancer-Chip revealed a 1000-fold difference in the concentration of TCB required to kill target cells.
source: We tested the same molecule in a healthy Lung-Chip versus a cancer-Chip and found a 1000-fold difference in the concentration of TCB required to kill target cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: An all-in-one platform could combine a healthy population with a tumor one in the same chip to capture safety liabilities triggered by tumor lysis itself.
source: As a next step, an all-in-one platform could combine a healthy population with a tumor one in the same chip as previously described (Hassell et al., 2017), thus capturing safety liabilities triggered by tumor lysis itself.
evidence: This is a statement about potential future developments of the platform, supported by a citation.

claim: Using a chip comprising only healthy tissue is a reasonable safety evaluation approach when the organ of concern is different from the cancer-affected organ.
source: Although efficacy–safety interactions are clinically relevant, these two aspects are often evaluated independently prior to phase I clinical studies, owing largely to the absence of fitting preclinical tools. We believe that using a chip comprising only healthy tissue is a reasonable safety evaluation approach in the case when the organ of concern is different from the cancer-affected organ.
evidence: This is a statement of the authors' opinion based on their experimental approach.

claim: The tumor microenvironment and anti-tumor efficacy effects might influence the toxicity outcome when the target-expressing organ and the tumor co-localize.
source: However, the tumor microenvironment and anti-tumor efficacy effects might influence the toxicity outcome when the target-expressing organ and the tumor co-localize, and should therefore be taken into account.
evidence: This is a logical inference about potential complications when tumor and at-risk organ are the same.

claim: Treating colorectal cancer with CEA-targeting TCBs may lead to an increased risk of intestinal toxicities.
source: For example, treating colorectal cancer with CEA-targeting TCBs may lead to an increased risk of intestinal toxicities, taking into consideration that tumor cell lysis may lead to the release of inflammatory cytokines and tumor antigens, thus further potentiating immune cell activation and cytotoxicity.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential risks based on the mechanism of action.

claim: The coupling of healthy and tumor biopsy-derived organoids with immunocompetent Organ-Chip technology may provide the ideal setup for a combined efficacy and safety assessment.
source: The coupling of healthy and tumor biopsy-derived organoids with immunocompetent Organ-Chip technology may provide the ideal setup for a combined efficacy and safety assessment.
evidence: This is a statement about potential future developments of the platform.

claim: The concepts introduced in this study can be expanded to address the persisting gap in modeling immune-related toxicities associated with immune checkpoint blockade.
source: Going forward, the concepts we introduced here can be expanded to address the persisting gap in modeling immune-related toxicities, associated with, for example, immune checkpoint blockade (Brahmer et al., 2018; Ramos-Casals et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a statement about potential future applications of the approach, supported by citations.

claim: Modeling immune checkpoint blockade toxicities accurately would likely require the incorporation of resident immune cells and lymphoid structures, as well as modalities that support the simulation of T-cell trafficking and tissue infiltration.
source: Considering their systemic and multifactorial immunopathology, modeling these processes accurately would likely require the incorporation of resident immune cells and lymphoid structures, as well as modalities that support the simulation of T-cell trafficking and tissue infiltration.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about requirements for future model development.
